title: The Turn That Did Not Happen, Except That It Did
description:
Tell the story of rejected turns, rollback, and retries.

Narrative hook and core question: What does it mean to reject an AI-generated turn after its tools have already changed the world?

Begin with the concrete failure: give_item successfully mutates state, the auditor rejects the candidate turn, repair/retry runs, and the supposedly rejected turn has already changed reality. Expand to repeated damage, resources consumed twice, duplicate combats and combatants, repeated inventory grants, exactly-once effects, speculative candidate execution versus committed turn, audit evidence, repair/retry lifecycle, rollback or transactional boundaries, and invariants showing that a rejected candidate plus repaired retry leaves one accepted world transition.

Expected architectural conclusion: an auditor cannot merely judge prose after the fact. Candidate execution, evidence, rollback, repair, and commit semantics form a transaction protocol.

Boundaries: focus on transactionality and audit lifecycle. Do not turn this into the general rules-pack story.

Use repository history, PRs, design docs, ADRs, audits, and playtest transcripts as evidence. Verify claims against artifacts, not model memory; distinguish implemented architecture from planned architecture; preserve static search-indexable public readability; and follow Joseph's voice rules: analytical and curious, concrete before abstraction, dry humor when earned, deliberate we/I attribution, reflect praise, absorb blame, no em dashes, and no generic LLM prose.
